summary: For ages 7–8, teach how fossils form as an ordered process story: an organism dies, is quickly buried in sediment, more layers pile on and press down, over millions of years sediment turns to rock while the organism's shape is preserved (often as minerals replace the material), and much later the rock is exposed and the fossil found. Two big ideas carry the most weight: burial must be QUICK (before the body rots or scatters) and fossilisation takes an ENORMOUS amount of time. Distinguish body fossils (shells, bones — shape preserved in stone) from trace fossils (footprints, imprints — evidence of activity). Link to prior learning that fossils occur mainly in sedimentary rock and that only once-living things fossilise. A driveable simulation of the process is proposed as the central activity, with sequencing/sorting practice, a retelling task, a tap-to-reveal cross-section, an optional excavation and expert Q&A, and a hands-on plaster-cast as complements. These are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
misconceptions: 'Fossils are the actual bones/animal, unchanged' — not knowing minerals replace/preserve the shape in rock.
'Fossils form quickly' — missing the millions-of-years timescale.
'Any dead thing becomes a fossil' — not realising it needs quick burial and the right conditions (most don't fossilise).
'Fossils are found in any rock' — rather than mainly sedimentary rock.
'A footprint isn't a fossil' — not recognising trace fossils.
'Dinosaurs and fossils are the same thing' — conflating one example with the whole concept.

activities.title: Fossil-formation time machine (drive the process)
steps: Place a dead organism (for example a shell or a small animal) on an ancient seabed.
Face a choice: bury it now or wait — if you wait too long, scavengers, decay and moving water can break up and scatter it so nothing is left to become a fossil; choose to bury it quickly.
Drag layer after layer of sediment on top of the buried organism.
Move a time slider to sweep across a very long time (millions of years) and watch soft mud compress and harden into rock while the organism's shape is preserved in stone.
Dig down and lift out the finished fossil.
Use a toggle to make a trace fossil instead: leave a footprint in the mud and fossilise that.
activities.insight: Fossilisation is a time-ordered process with a hidden mechanism; quick burial is essential (waiting too long usually means the remains are rotted, broken up or scattered before they can be preserved) and the process takes an unimaginably long time. The shape is preserved in rock rather than the unchanged original surviving.

activities.title: Sequence and sort the fossil facts
steps: Put the five fossilisation stages in order: organism dies → buried quickly in mud/sand → layers build up and press down → sediment turns to rock over millions of years (shape preserved) → rock exposed and fossil found.
Sort example cards into body fossils (shell, bone) versus trace fossils (footprint, imprint).
Answer how long fossils take to form: days, years, or millions of years (millions of years).
activities.insight: Consolidate the ordered sequence, the body-vs-trace distinction, and the vast timescale.

activities.title: Retell the fossil story and explain the conditions
steps: In your own words, retell the fossil-formation sequence in order, from the organism dying to the fossil being found.
Explain why most dead things — like leaves that fall in a park every autumn — do NOT become fossils.
State what has to happen to the dead animal or plant first, before it can become a fossil.
Describe whether a shell fossil found in rock is the unchanged original shell or something else, and how a shell ended up inside rock.
activities.insight: A full explanation names burial in sediment, layers building up, sediment turning to rock over millions of years with the shape preserved, and why fossilisation is rare.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal cross-section of the stages
steps: Tap each layer/stage of a layered cross-section scene to reveal a caption explaining what is happening at that step.
Open a lift-the-flap labelled 'Why must it be buried quickly?' and read the explanation.
activities.insight: The sequence and vocabulary of fossil formation, presented as a labelled cross-section through the sediment layers.

activities.title: Plaster cast of a shell (hands-on)
steps: Press a shell firmly into clay or plasticine to leave a clear imprint, then remove the shell.
Pour plaster into the imprint and let it set.
Lift out the plaster and compare its shape to the original shell.
activities.insight: The surrounding material can keep the SHAPE of an object even after the original is gone — a concrete analogy for how rock preserves a fossil's shape.

activities.title: Ask the palaeontologist (optional extension)
steps: Ask an in-role palaeontologist 'why/how' questions, such as 'Why don't most animals become fossils?' or 'How did this particular fossil form?'
Use the answers to deepen your understanding of the conditions needed for fossilisation.
activities.insight: Fossils are rare and depend on specific conditions (quick burial, the right environment); curiosity-driven questions can deepen the conditions idea.

activities.title: 3D excavation (optional engagement extra)
steps: After a fossil has formed, rotate the rock and carefully extract the fossil from it in a 3D dig.
Observe how the fossil sits embedded in the surrounding rock.
activities.insight: Fossils are embedded in rock and uncovered by excavation; this adds realism to the 'exposed and found' stage.

checkQuestion: A fossil of a shell is found inside solid rock. Is that the actual original shell that was there millions of years ago, or something else? And how did a shell end up inside rock in the first place?
checkAnswer: It's usually not the unchanged original. The shell was buried in mud or sand, more layers piled on top, and over millions of years the sediment turned to rock while the shell's shape was preserved (often the material is slowly replaced by minerals). So the rock kept the SHAPE of the shell over a very long time.
